title: Who Actually Answers When You Call 911 #shorts
summary: In 2021, 49 states reported 4,637 primary public safety answering points, run by local or state government; for landlines a router picks the center and a database adds the address.
sources: 2021 data: 45 states reported 213,652,929 total 911 calls; 49 states reported 4,637 primary PSAPs; 38 states reported 507,969 texts to 911 (NHTSA National 911 Program, National 911 Annual Report: 2021 Data): https://www.911.gov/assets/2021-911-Profile-Database-Report_FINAL.pdf

The US 911 system is operated by local and state government; where text-to-911 is not available, the sender gets a bounce-back message (911.gov, Frequently asked questions): https://911.gov/calling-911/frequently-asked-questions

The selective router directs a 911 call to the appropriate PSAP; the PSAP equipment sends the caller's number (ANI) to the 911 database, which performs an ALI (automatic location identification) look-up and returns the caller's location to the call taker (California Governor's Office of Emergency Services, 9-1-1 system description, chapter II): https://www.caloes.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/PSC/Documents/Chapter-II-System-Description.pdf

scenes.narration: In {2021|twenty twenty-one}, {49|forty-nine} states reported {4,637|four thousand six hundred thirty-seven} primary {911|nine one one} centers.
Each one is a public safety answering point, run by local or state government.
On a landline, a router reads the number and picks the right center. A database puts the address on screen.
So a landline already knows where you are.
